export function validAI(out, ctx) {
  if (!out || typeof out.hi !== 'string' || typeof out.en !== 'string') return false
  if (!hasDevanagari(out.hi) || out.hi.length > 400 || out.en.length > 400) return false
  // No answer reveal while the learner is still trying.
  // Jaanch must not call a wrong answer right.
  if (ctx?.agent === 'jaanch' && ctx.verdict === 'wrong' && /\b(correct|right)\b/i.test(out.en) && !/\b(not|isn't|incorrect|wrong)\b/i.test(out.en)) return false
  if (ctx?.verdict !== 'correct' && (ctx?.attempt || 0) < 2 && ctx?.task?.correct != null) {
    const c = String(Math.abs(ctx.task.correct))
    const re = new RegExp(`=\\s*[−-]?\\s*${c}(?!\\d)`)
    if (re.test(out.hi) || re.test(out.en)) return false
    // Also block the bare answer number when it is not already in the question (e.g. "you get 8").
    const inQuestion = new RegExp(`(^|\\D)${c}(?!\\d)`).test(String(ctx.task.expr || ''))
    const bare = new RegExp(`(^|\\D)${c}(?!\\d)`)
    if (!inQuestion && (bare.test(out.en) || bare.test(out.hi))) return false
    // Block rewriting into the easy sum, e.g. "5 + 3".
    const sums = [...out.en.matchAll(/(\d+)\s*\+\s*(\d+)/g)]
    if (sums.some((m) => +m[1] + +m[2] === Math.abs(ctx.task.correct))) return false
    // Block computing it in words: "₹3 more than ₹5".
    if (/\d+\s*(more|less|bigger|smaller|greater|fewer)\s+than\s*₹?\s*\d+/i.test(out.en)) return false
  }
  return true
}
export async function aiTurn(ctx, fallback, timeoutMs = 11000) {
  if (typeof navigator !== 'undefined' && navigator.onLine === false) return { ...fallback, source: 'scripted' }
  const ctrl = new AbortController()
  const timer = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), timeoutMs)
  try {
    const r = await fetch('/api/agent', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(ctx),
      signal: ctrl.signal,
    })
    const j = await r.json()
    if (j.ok && validAI(j, ctx)) return { hi: j.hi, en: j.en, score: j.score, stance: j.stance, source: 'ai', model: j.model }
  } catch {
    /* fall through to scripted */
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer)
  }
  return { ...fallback, source: 'scripted' }

Here's how it works in the code as it stands now, including the other agent's changes from the last few minutes.

## Who does what

| Part | Is it AI? | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **Checker** (`check()` in `src/agents.js`) | No, plain code | Decides if the answer is right, and which misconception it matches (M1, M2, `diff`, `sign`, `other`) |
| **Jaanch** (Evaluator) | AI | Tells the learner the verdict in words and names the misconception |
| **Samjhao** (Explainer) | AI | Gives a hint matched to the misconception: the udhaar (shop credit) story for M1, number-line direction for M2 |
| **Sawaal** (Challenger) | AI | Asks one "why?" question or gives a counterexample; can disagree with Jaanch |
| **Coordinator** (`Practice.jsx` / `TwoViews.jsx`) | No, plain code | Decides who speaks and in what order, passes messages between agents, checks AI output |
| **Teacher** (S6) | Human | Has the final say on disagreements and on scores for free-text answers |

All three agents run through one serverless endpoint, `api/agent.js`. They share common rules (`COMMON`, `CONVO`), and each has its own role prompt (`ROLES`). The model chain is Groq `gpt-oss-120b`, then `gpt-oss-20b`, then Gemini flash-lite with key 1, then key 2, within a 10-second budget.

## Flow of one answer (S3 Practice)

```
Learner submits an answer
  │
  ▼
1. CHECKER (code)   check(task, ans) → { correct, tag: 'M2' }
  │                 shows "✗ Not right yet" straight away (no AI wait)
  ▼
2. BLACKBOARD       blackboard(progress) → past tasks with their misconception tags,
  │                 plus a count of how often M1 and M2 have appeared
  ▼
3. COORDINATOR      picks speakers from the script for this tag: task.feedback['M2'] = [Jaanch, Samjhao]
  │                 resets the conversation, then runs the agents one after another:
  │
  ├─► JAANCH   gets: task, verdict, tag, attempt, blackboard, scripted line, conversation = []
  │            "The answer isn't +7, looks like 'two minuses = plus' got used."
  │            ── its message is added to the conversation ──
  │
  └─► SAMJHAO  gets: the same input + conversation = [Jaanch's message]
               reads Jaanch's diagnosis and builds on it: "Here a negative is ADDED: ₹4 owed + ₹3 owed…"
               also returns stance: agree or disagree with Jaanch
  │
  ▼
4. VALIDATOR (code, validAI)  checks each AI reply before the learner sees it:
     has Hindi, under 400 characters, Jaanch never calls a wrong answer right,
     no answer leak before the 2nd attempt (no "= 7", no bare 7,
     no "5 + 3", no "3 more than 5")
     fails or takes longer than 11 s → the scripted line written in advance is shown instead
  │
  ▼
5. Learner retries, asks for a hint, or asks a question ("Explain it to me" → Samjhao,
   "challenge me" → Sawaal); the question goes in as learner_question along with the conversation so far
```

## How the agents exchange information (the P3 requirement)

1. **Conversation passing.** Each agent's reply is added to `convo.current` and sent to the next agent, which sees the last 4 turns. The prompt tells each agent to react to the others by name, e.g. "जाँच ने सही कहा…".
2. **Shared blackboard.** Every agent gets the learner's history, including which earlier questions showed M1 or M2. Sawaal uses it to say things like "in question 1 you used this same rule wrongly".
3. **Stance signal.** Every agent returns `agree` or `disagree` about the previous message. When it's `disagree`, the bubble shows "🤝 Disagrees with Jaanch".
4. **The debate (S4, `TwoViews.jsx`).** On T5 the learner picks reason B, the memorised "two minuses make a plus" shortcut. Jaanch's AI reply is passed to Sawaal with `debate: true`, and Sawaal must disagree and name the counterexample −2 + (−5). The coordinator then shows one "Two views: you decide" card with three choices: test it, keep my reason, or ask the teacher.
5. **Results feed back.** If the test fails, an M2 tag is added to T5, which lowers the LO2 result and shows on the teacher's class table. If the learner asks the teacher, the item goes to the review queue. The teacher's decision appears as a message on S5 the next time the learner opens the app.

## Weak spots an examiner could catch (`DESIGN.md` overclaims)

- **The diagnosis is code, not Jaanch.** `DESIGN.md` says "Jaanch writes stance + diagnosis to the blackboard". In the code, the checker writes the misconception tag and Jaanch only puts it into words. That's deliberate (correctness is never left to AI), but describe it as "the code diagnoses, Jaanch explains it".
- **The blackboard is rebuilt, not written to.** Agents don't write to it directly. It's rebuilt from saved progress each turn. Agents pass messages through the conversation.
- **Agents don't remember earlier questions in conversation.** The conversation resets on every submit. Memory across questions comes only from the blackboard's tags.
- **The teacher's decision doesn't change agent feedback.** `DESIGN.md` says a teacher override "replaces the agents' feedback". In the code, it only shows as a message on the S5 progress screen.

why does pause buttons take me to the front page

----- [2026-11-18 14:07:12] ASSISTANT -----
It's by design, but the label is misleading. Pause runs `exit()` in `src/App.jsx`, which logs `session_end`, signs the learner out and goes back to S1 (Start).

The idea came from the learner's situation: it's a parent's phone that can be taken back at any moment. Pause saves progress on the phone, frees the screen, and next time the child taps their name under "Already on this phone" to pick up on the same card or question. So it really works as **"Save and exit"**, while the button says Pause.

A child who taps "Pause" expects to come back to the same place, not the front page. I'd fix it one of two ways:

1. **A real pause screen (recommended).** Pause covers the screen with a calm "Paused · your progress is saved" message, a big **Resume** button that returns to exactly where they were, and a small **"Done for today"** link under it that exits to Start. It keeps the shared-phone exit and uses the same "big main button, small option below" pattern you liked. It's about 25 lines in `App.jsx` plus some CSS.
2. **Rename only.** Change the button to "💾 Save & exit" (Hindi: "सेव करके बाहर"), so the label matches what it does. It's a one-line change.

Should I build option 1 and deploy it?

const freshSession = () => ({ screen: 'S2', cardIdx: 0, taskIdx: 0, order: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], progress: {} })

export default function App() {
  const [lang, setLang] = useState(() => store.read('gc_lang_v2', 'en'))
  const [screen, setScreen] = useState('S1')
  const [learner, setLearner] = useState(null)
  const [session, setSession] = useState(null)

  const t = (o) => (o && typeof o === 'object' ? (o[lang] ?? o.hi) : o)

  useEffect(() => {
    store.write('gc_lang_v2', lang)
    document.documentElement.lang = lang
  }, [lang])
  useEffect(() => {
    store.logEvent('page_view', { target: screen })
    window.scrollTo(0, 0)
  }, [screen])

  function updateSession(patch) {
    setSession((s) => {
      const next = { ...s, ...(typeof patch === 'function' ? patch(s) : patch) }
      if (learner) store.saveSession(learner.id, next)
      return next
    })
  }

  function go(to) {
    setScreen(to)
    if (learner && to !== 'S6' && to !== 'S1') updateSession({ screen: to })
  }

  function startLearner(name) {
    const l = store.upsertLearner(name)
    store.setUser(l.id)
    const s = store.loadSession(l.id) || freshSession()
    store.saveSession(l.id, s)
    setLearner(l)
    setSession(s)
    store.logEvent('session_start', { meta: { resumed: Object.keys(s.progress || {}).length > 0, lang } })
    setScreen(s.screen || 'S2')
  }

  function exit() {
    store.logEvent('session_end', { target: screen })
    store.setUser('anon')
    setLearner(null)
    setSession(null)
    setScreen('S1')
  }

  const props = { t, lang, go, learner, session, updateSession }

  return (
    <div className="app">
      <header className="top">
        <div className="brand">{lang === 'hi' ? 'गणित चौपाल' : 'Ganit Chaupal'}</div>
        <div className="token" title="Identity token">
          ID {ROLL} · {screen} {t(SCREENS[screen])}
        </div>
        <div className="top-actions">
          <button className="chip" onClick={() => setLang(lang === 'hi' ? 'en' : 'hi')} aria-label="Language">
            {lang === 'hi' ? 'EN' : 'हिं'}
          </button>
          {(learner || screen === 'S6') && (
            <button className="chip" onClick={exit}>
              {t({ hi: '⏸ रुको', en: '⏸ Pause' })}
            </button>
          )}
        </div>
      </header>

      {learner && screen !== 'S6' && (
        <nav className="steps">
          {['S2', 'S3', 'S5'].map((s) => (
            <button key={s} className={screen === s || (s === 'S3' && screen === 'S4') ? 'on' : ''} onClick={() => go(s)}>
              {t(SCREENS[s])}
            </button>
          ))}
        </nav>
      )}

      <main className="main">
        {screen === 'S1' && <Start {...props} onStart={startLearner} onTeacher={() => setScreen('S6')} />}
        {screen === 'S2' && session && <Learn {...props} />}
        {screen === 'S3' && session && <Practice key={session.taskIdx + '-' + session.order.join('')} {...props} />}
        {screen === 'S4' && session && <TwoViews {...props} />}
        {screen === 'S5' && session && <Summary {...props} />}
        {screen === 'S6' && <Teacher {...props} />}
      </main>

      <footer className="foot">

      </footer>
    </div>
  )
}

**Card:** P3 Multi-agent collaborative learning · T1 Integers: operations with negative numbers (Class 7) ·
L1 Rural government school, regional-language medium, parent's Android phone for about 30 min in the evening ·
C5 Teacher-in-the-loop
**Author:** Tushar Bajaj (23B2107) · **Live app:** https://et617-23b2107.vercel.app

*Chaupal* is the village meeting place where people discuss a matter and each person states their view. In the app,
three AI agents discuss the learner's answer, and **the learner decides**.

> **Language:** the learner sees **Hindi first**, with an English toggle. Hindi is the regional medium of instruction in
> our assumed setting, rural Madhya Pradesh. The Hindi lines below are the exact text shown in the app; the English
> lines (in italics) are translations for evaluators.

**Shared system prompt (`COMMON`):**
```text
You are one of three AI agents in "Ganit Chaupal", a maths practice app for a 12-year-old Class 7 student in a rural Hindi-medium government school in India. Topic: adding and subtracting negative integers.
Agents: Jaanch (evaluator), Samjhao (explainer), Sawaal (challenger). You receive a BLACKBOARD (JSON) written by a code checker and the other agents.
Rules:
- The checker's verdict is FINAL. Never contradict it. Never call a wrong answer right.
- Use only two models: the number line (left/right steps) and "udhaar" (shop credit; a negative number = money owed).
- At most 2 short sentences. Simple Hindi in Devanagari that a Class 7 Hindi-medium student knows; digits and + − = are fine.
- Address the learner as "तुम". Avoid gendered verb forms for the learner (prefer "तुमने ..." or impersonal forms).
- If the verdict is "wrong" and attempt < 2, do NOT state the final answer.

[TOOL RESULT]
export function reviewToRow(r) {
  const { id, learnerId, learnerName, taskId, kind, status, decision, message, ts, decidedAt, ...payload } = r
  return { id, learner_id: learnerId, learner_name: learnerName, task_id: taskId, kind, status, decision: decision ?? null, message: message ?? null, payload, created_at: ts, decided_at: decidedAt ?? null }
}
export function rowToReview(x) {
  return { ...x.payload, id: x.id, learnerId: x.learner_id, learnerName: x.learner_name, taskId: x.task_id, kind: x.kind, status: x.status, decision: x.decision, message: x.message, ts: x.created_at, decidedAt: x.decided_at }
}
export async function fetchReviews(learnerId) {
  const q = 'reviews?select=*&order=created_at.desc&limit=200' + (learnerId ? `&learner_id=eq.${encodeURIComponent(learnerId)}` : '')
  return (await rest(q)).map(rowToReview)
}
export async function fetchLearners() {
  return rest('learners?select=id,name,progress,last_active&order=last_active.desc&limit=200')
}
export async function fetchEvents() {
  return rest('events?select=ts,user_id,session_id,event_type,target,objective_id,value,correct,duration_ms,meta&order=ts.desc&limit=2000')
}

create table if not exists public.learners (
  id text primary key, name text not null, progress jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb,
  created_at timestamptz default now(), last_active timestamptz default now()
);
create table if not exists public.events (
  id bigint generated always as identity primary key, ts timestamptz not null, user_id text not null,
  session_id text not null, event_type text not null, target text, objective_id text, value text,
  correct boolean, duration_ms integer, meta jsonb default '{}'::jsonb, received_at timestamptz default now()
);
create index if not exists events_user_idx on public.events (user_id, ts);
create index if not exists events_type_idx on public.events (event_type);
create table if not exists public.reviews (
  id text primary key, learner_id text not null, learner_name text, task_id text,
  kind text not null check (kind in ('disagreement','freetext')), status text not null default 'pending',
  payload jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb, decision text, message jsonb,
  created_at timestamptz default now(), decided_at timestamptz
);
create index if not exists reviews_learner_idx on public.reviews (learner_id);

// Offline cache for weak evening signal: app shell is cache-first, /api is never cached.
const CACHE = 'gc-v1'
self.addEventListener('install', (e) => {
  e.waitUntil(caches.open(CACHE).then((c) => c.addAll(['/', '/index.html', '/favicon.svg', '/manifest.webmanifest'])))
  self.skipWaiting()
})
self.addEventListener('activate', (e) => {
  e.waitUntil(caches.keys().then((ks) => Promise.all(ks.filter((k) => k !== CACHE).map((k) => caches.delete(k)))))
  self.clients.claim()
})
self.addEventListener('fetch', (e) => {
  const url = new URL(e.request.url)
  if (e.request.method !== 'GET' || url.pathname.startsWith('/api/')) return
  // Pages: network first (fresh deploys), fall back to cache offline. Assets and fonts: cache first.
  if (e.request.mode === 'navigate') {
    e.respondWith(fetch(e.request).then((r) => { caches.open(CACHE).then((c) => c.put('/', r.clone())); return r }).catch(() => caches.match('/')))
    return
  }
  e.respondWith(
    caches.match(e.request).then((hit) => hit || fetch(e.request).then((r) => {
      if (r.ok || r.type === 'opaque') { const copy = r.clone(); caches.open(CACHE).then((c) => c.put(e.request, copy)) }
      return r
    })),
  )

----- [2026-11-18 14:33:11] ASSISTANT -----
The agents now respond properly, and the fix is live (commit `c4ed3bd`).

**What was wrong:** the agents were falling back to the scripted hint instead of replying, which is why it looked like they weren't talking to each other. Your 3 keys weren't the problem; all three work and the app already tries them in order. There were two causes:
- **My earlier change used up the reply budget.** The "medium reasoning" setting I added made the model spend its whole token allowance thinking, so all 3 keys returned nothing.
- **The safety check threw away whole replies.** Step-by-step answers counted all the way to "−7", and the check that stops the app giving away the answer discarded the entire reply.

**What changed:**
- **Speed:** back to fast reasoning, so replies come from Groq in 1–2 seconds instead of 10–15 seconds through Gemini.
- **Answer number hidden, not discarded:** a reply like "−5, −6, then ?" is kept and the child works out the last step.
- **Explains the other agents:** when the child says "I don't get what Sawaal is asking", Samjhao now replies "Sawaal is asking: why do we move left when we add −3?" and walks through it.

**Tested:** I replayed your exact conversation 3 times against the live site, using a local copy of the app's reply checks. All 3 were real AI replies, none leaked the answer, and none fell back to the scripted hint. I haven't re-tested it by clicking through the app.

7	**Card:** P3 Multi-agent collaborative learning · T1 Integers: operations with negative numbers (Class 7) ·
8	L1 Rural government school, regional-language medium, parent's Android phone for about 30 min in the evening ·
9	C5 Teacher-in-the-loop
10	**Author:** Tushar Bajaj (23B2107) · **Live app:** https://et617-23b2107.vercel.app
11	
12	*Chaupal* is the village meeting place where people discuss a matter and each person states their view. In the app,
13	three AI agents discuss the learner's answer, and **the learner decides**.
14	
15	> **Language:** every screen is in Hindi and English with a one-tap toggle (the app opens in English; the choice is
16	> remembered on the phone). Hindi is the regional medium of instruction in our assumed setting, rural Madhya Pradesh. The Hindi lines below are the exact text shown in the app; the English
17	> lines (in italics) are translations for evaluators.

21	## D1. Educational problem
22	
23	### Problem
24	In rural Hindi-medium government schools, Class 7 learners mostly meet integer operations as memorised sign rules
25	("minus-minus is plus"), without a picture of what a negative number means. As a result they make two predictable
26	errors:
27	- treating subtraction of a negative like subtraction of a positive: **5 − (−3) = 2**
28	- stretching "two minuses make a plus" to addition: **−4 + (−3) = 7**
29	
30	One maths teacher handles Classes 6–8, and parents often cannot help with this topic, so these errors go unnoticed until
31	test papers are marked. The learner's only practice window is about 30 minutes on a parent's Android phone in the
32	evening, on weak, shared prepaid data. The learner needs practice that makes them **reason, not just answer**, catches
33	the misconception when it appears, and lets the teacher see and correct the AI's feedback the next day.
34	
35	### Learning outcomes
36	
37	| # | After the activity, the learner will be able to… | Bloom level (revised) | Measured by | Success criterion |
38	|---|---|---|---|---|
39	| **LO1** | **Predict** the sign of, and **compute**, the result of adding or subtracting integers that include negative numbers, e.g. −4 + (−3), 5 − (−3) | Apply | Tasks T1–T4 plus one check item | ≥ 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt |
40	| **LO2** | **Explain**, using a number-line move or an *udhaar* (shop-credit) story, why subtracting a negative number makes the result larger, e.g. 5 − (−3) = 8 | Understand | Task T5 (choose a reason, then explain in own words) | Picks the meaning-based reason, **or** scores ≥ 2/3 on the explanation rubric |
41	| **LO3** | **Compare** two worked solutions, **identify** the wrong one, and **name** the misconception it uses | Evaluate | Task T6, plus the check item in the "two views" moment | Correct choice **with** the correct reason |
42	
43	### Context of use
44	- **Where:** at home in the village, often with siblings and family around. Sound can't be relied on, and the learner
45	  may be interrupted.
46	- **When:** about 7:30–8:00 pm, after the parent returns from the fields and hands over the phone; about 30 minutes, and
47	  the phone may be taken back for a call at any time.
48	- **Device:** the parent's low-cost Android phone (about 6.5″ screen, 2–3 GB RAM, Chrome), on a shared daily prepaid data
49	  pack with a weak 4G/3G signal indoors.
50	- **Teacher (C5):** reviews the class on her own phone in the staff room the next morning, and approves or overrides
51	  AI feedback before the learner's next evening session.

55	## D2. Learner persona: Kavita, 12
56	
57	| Field | Kavita |
58	|---|---|
59	| **Name, age, class** | Kavita, 12, Class 7, Government Middle School in a village in Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh *(location assumed)* |

61	| **Device** | Father's Android phone, about ₹7,000, 6.5″ screen, 2–3 GB RAM, Chrome. Shared daily prepaid data; the signal drops indoors in the evening. |
62	| **Time** | About 30 minutes, roughly 7:30–8:00 pm, after her father returns. Often cut short when he needs the phone. |
63	| **Language** | Hindi at home and at school (Hindi-medium). Reads Devanagari comfortably and knows the textbook terms *ऋणात्मक* (negative), *धनात्मक* (positive), *संख्या रेखा* (number line). Writes digits and + − = as in the textbook. Reads only a little English. |
64	| **Prior knowledge of prerequisites** | **Secure:** whole-number addition and subtraction; reading a number line; placing −3 on a number line and knowing −5 °C means "below zero" (met integers in Class 6, *assumed*). **Shaky:** ordering negatives (thinks −8 > −3 "because 8 > 3"); adding numbers with mixed signs. **Memorised without meaning:** "minus-minus is plus", picked up from class and an older cousin. |
65	| **Primary goal (her words)** | "माइनस वाले सवालों में बार-बार गलती होती है। मुझे समझना है कि कब प्लस बनता है।" *"I keep making mistakes in minus questions. I want to understand when it becomes plus."* |
66	| **Biggest barrier** | When she is stuck at home, there is nobody to ask. Her two memorised rules conflict, and she can't tell which one applies. |
67	| **Motivation** | Wants to stop losing marks on "minus" questions in the half-yearly exam. Enjoys being trusted with the phone for "real" study. Likes being asked her opinion. **Gives up** after 2–3 wrong attempts with no explanation, and goes quiet when corrected in front of others. |
68	| **Theory link** | *Rules learned without meaning* → she needs concrete models (number line plus a money story; situated learning, dual coding). *Stuck without a tutor* → hints at the moment she is stuck (ZPD, scaffolding). *Fear of being wrong* → private, encouraging feedback (affective filter). *Two conflicting rules* → let her resolve the conflict herself, with evidence (cognitive conflict and conceptual change, Posner et al., 1982). *30-minute window* → small chunks, one task per screen (Cognitive Load Theory). |
69	
70	### Two likely misconceptions
71	
72	| | **M1: "Subtracting always makes it smaller"** (घटाने से हमेशा छोटा) | **M2: "Two minuses make a plus, everywhere"** (दो माइनस = प्लस, हर जगह) |
73	|---|---|---|
74	| **What she does** | Ignores the sign of the number being subtracted, so a − (−b) becomes a − b | Makes the answer positive whenever two minus signs appear, including in addition |
75	| **Typical wrong answers** | 5 − (−3) = **2** · −2 − (−6) = **−8** · 6 − (−2) = **4** | −4 + (−3) = **7** · −40 + (−25) = **65** · −2 − (−6) = **8** |
76	| **Why it arises** | Years of whole-number experience, where subtraction always makes the number smaller | A sign rule memorised without meaning (from −(−b) or from multiplication) and applied beyond where it holds |
77	| **How the app detects it** | The learner's answer equals the answer M1 would predict for that item | The learner's answer equals the answer M2 would predict, **or** they choose the rule-only reason in T5 and then fail the check item |
78	
79	M1 *under*-applies the sign change and M2 *over*-applies it. The same learner can show both, which is why the agents
80	must share what each one has observed.

83	*7:40 pm. After dinner her father hands her his phone. She taps the "Ganit Chaupal" shortcut on the home screen. The
84	app remembers her from yesterday, with no password, and opens on the task she left. The signal drops twice, but the
85	tasks are already loaded, so she keeps going. When she writes −4 + (−3) = 7, the agents don't just say "wrong". The
86	number line shows her arrow going left, and Samjhao tells the udhaar story. At 8:05 her father needs the phone. She taps

97	## D3. Educational content: one complete learning activity
98	
99	**Activity:** उधार और संख्या रेखा: ऋणात्मक संख्याओं का जोड़-घटाना
100	*(Udhaar and the number line: adding and subtracting negative numbers)*
101	**Duration:** about 20 minutes (concept about 5 min, 6 tasks about 12 min, summary about 2 min), which fits the 30-minute window.
102	
103	**Who speaks** (three AI agents with distinct roles):
104	
105	| Agent | Role | Speaks when |
106	|---|---|---|
107	| ✅ **Jaanch** (जाँच, "check") | Evaluator. States whether the answer is correct (verified by code, never by AI), names the misconception, judges the quality of explanations | After every attempt |
108	| 🧭 **Samjhao** (समझाओ, "explain") | Explainer. Number line and udhaar story, chosen to fit the misconception Jaanch found | After a wrong attempt, on a hint request, or to reconcile a disagreement |
109	| ❓ **Sawaal** (सवाल, "question") | Challenger. Asks "why?", offers counterexamples and extension questions, tests whether a rule really holds | After a correct attempt, or when the reasoning looks memorised |
110	
111	### Part A: Concept explanation (4 short cards, each with an interactive number line from −10 to 10)
112	
113	**Card 1: ऋणात्मक संख्या क्या है? (What is a negative number?)**
114	> संख्या रेखा पर 0 के दाईं ओर धनात्मक संख्याएँ (1, 2, 3…) हैं और बाईं ओर ऋणात्मक संख्याएँ (−1, −2, −3…)। −3 यानी 0 से
115	> 3 कदम बाईं ओर। पैसों में सोचो: **+5** = तुम्हारे पास ₹5 हैं। **−3** = तुम पर दुकान का ₹3 उधार है।
116	>
117	> *On the number line, positive numbers (1, 2, 3…) are right of 0 and negative numbers (−1, −2, −3…) are left. −3 means
118	> 3 steps left of 0. Think in money: +5 = you have ₹5. −3 = you owe the shop ₹3 (udhaar).*
119	> **Quick check (not scored):** "−3 पर टैप करो" *(Tap −3)*
120	
121	**Card 2: जोड़ना = संख्या की दिशा में चलो (Adding = move in the number's direction)**
122	> धनात्मक संख्या जोड़ो → दाईं ओर चलो। ऋणात्मक संख्या जोड़ो → बाईं ओर चलो।
123	> उदाहरण: **2 + (−5)** → 2 से 5 कदम बाईं ओर → **−3**
124	> उदाहरण: **−1 + (−4)** → −1 से 4 कदम और बाईं ओर → **−5**
125	> पैसों में: उधार में उधार जोड़ो तो उधार बढ़ता है। ₹1 उधार + ₹4 उधार = ₹5 उधार, यानी −5 (+5 नहीं!)
126	>
127	> *Add a positive → move right. Add a negative → move left. 2 + (−5) = −3. −1 + (−4) = −5. In money: udhaar added to
128	> udhaar makes a bigger udhaar: ₹1 owed + ₹4 owed = ₹5 owed, i.e. −5 (not +5!)*
129	
130	**Card 3: घटाना = उल्टी दिशा में चलो (Subtracting = move the opposite way)**
131	> किसी संख्या को घटाने का मतलब है उसकी उल्टी दिशा में चलना।
132	> उदाहरण: **−3 − 2** → 2 दाईं ओर वाली संख्या है; घटाना है, तो उल्टा: 2 कदम बाईं ओर → **−5**
133	> उदाहरण: **4 − (−2)** → −2 बाईं ओर वाली संख्या है; घटाना है, तो उल्टा: 2 कदम दाईं ओर → **6**
134	> पैसों में: तुम्हारे पास ₹6 हैं और दुकान का ₹2 उधार है, तो हिसाब 6 + (−2) = ₹4। दुकानदार ₹2 का उधार माफ़ कर दे, यानी
135	> उधार घटा दे: 4 − (−2) = ₹6। **उधार हटने से हिसाब बढ़ता है!**
136	>
137	> *Subtracting a number means moving opposite to its direction. −3 − 2 = −5 (2 points right, so go left).
138	> 4 − (−2) = 6 (−2 points left, so go right). In money: you have ₹6 and owe ₹2, so your account is 6 + (−2) = ₹4. If
139	> the shopkeeper waives the ₹2 udhaar (subtracts it): 4 − (−2) = ₹6. Removing a debt raises your account!*
140	
141	**Card 4: "दो माइनस = प्लस" कब सही है? (When is "two minuses = plus" true?)**
142	> ✔ **− (−3) = +3**: ऋणात्मक संख्या घटाना = दाईं ओर चलना।
143	> ✘ **+ (−3) ≠ +3**: ऋणात्मक संख्या जोड़ना = बाईं ओर चलना। उत्तर और ऋणात्मक होता है।
144	> ✘ **−4 − 3 ≠ +7**: यहाँ धनात्मक 3 घटाया जा रहा है: 3 कदम बाईं ओर → −7।
145	> हर सवाल से पहले खुद से पूछो: **दाईं ओर जाना है या बाईं ओर?**
146	>
147	> *✔ −(−3) = +3, because subtracting a negative = moving right. ✘ +(−3) is not +3: adding a negative = moving left.
148	> ✘ −4 − 3 is not +7: a positive 3 is subtracted, 3 steps left gives −7. Before every question ask: right or left?*
149

## D6. AI functionality specification

**Where the AI sits.** Code (`check()` in `src/agents.js`) decides whether an answer is right and which misconception
it matches. The AI never decides correctness. Three AI agents put that decision into words, explain, and challenge.
All AI calls go through one serverless endpoint, `api/agent.js`, so API keys never reach the phone.

**Model call (all features).**
- Chain, tried in order within a 10 s server budget: Groq `openai/gpt-oss-120b` (about 1 s) → Groq `openai/gpt-oss-20b`
  → Gemini `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` (key 1) → the same model (key 2).
- Groq: `temperature 0.4`, `reasoning_effort "low"`, `max_completion_tokens 600`, `response_format json_object`.
  Gemini: `temperature 0.4`, `maxOutputTokens 1024`, `responseMimeType application/json`.
- System prompt = `COMMON` + the agent's role prompt (below). User message = the blackboard JSON:

```json
{ "task": {"id": "T1", "expr": "−4 + (−3) = ?", "correct": -7},
  "verdict": "wrong", "misconception_tag": "M2", "attempt": 1, "learner_answer": 7,
  "blackboard": {"history": [{"task": "T1", "no": 1, "lo": "LO1", "tags": ["M2"], "done": false}, "…"],
                 "misconceptions": {"M1": 0, "M2": 1}},
  "reference_line": {"hi": "उत्तर +7 नहीं है। लगता है \"दो माइनस = प्लस\" वाला नियम यहाँ लग गया।", "en": "…"},
  "conversation": [], "learner_question": null }
```

**Shared system prompt (`COMMON`):**
```text
You are one of three AI agents in "Ganit Chaupal", a maths practice app for a 12-year-old Class 7 student in a rural Hindi-medium government school in India. Topic: adding and subtracting negative integers.
Agents: Jaanch (evaluator), Samjhao (explainer), Sawaal (challenger). You receive a BLACKBOARD (JSON) written by a code checker and the other agents.
Rules:
- The checker's verdict is FINAL. Never contradict it. Never call a wrong answer right.
- Use only two models: the number line (left/right steps) and "udhaar" (shop credit; a negative number = money owed).
- At most 2 short sentences. Simple Hindi in Devanagari that a Class 7 Hindi-medium student knows; digits and + − = are fine.
- Address the learner as "तुम". Avoid gendered verb forms for the learner (prefer "तुमने ..." or impersonal forms).
- If the verdict is "wrong" and attempt < 2, do NOT state the final answer.
- Stay consistent with the reference line from the teacher-approved script, but personalise using the learner's attempt and history.
Return ONLY JSON: {"hi": "<Hindi>", "en": "<English translation>"}
```

**Added for the three conversational agents (`CONVO`):**
```text
You can see the CONVERSATION so far (messages from the other agents and the learner). Respond to it: refer to another agent by name when you build on or disagree with them (e.g. "जाँच ने सही कहा…" / "मैं जाँच से सहमत नहीं…").
Speak as yourself in the first person; never mention your own name. Never mention "the checker" or "the check"; just state things directly.
While the learner has not yet answered correctly: never write the final answer, never compute it in words (e.g. "3 more than 5"), and never rewrite the question into an easier sum (e.g. "5 + 3"). Point only at the DIRECTION (left/right) or the udhaar idea and let the learner finish.
If "learner_question" is present, the learner asked YOU directly: actually answer their "why/what" with the number line or udhaar idea (Samjhao: a short explanation; Sawaal: a short explanation plus one guiding question back). Never give the final answer of the current question.
Return ONLY JSON: {"hi": "<Hindi>", "en": "<English>", "stance": "agree" | "disagree"}  (stance = do you agree with the previous agent's message; "agree" if there is none)
```

**Checks before the learner sees any AI line.**
1. Server (`api/agent.js`): the reply must parse as JSON with string `hi` and `en`, and `hi` must contain Devanagari.
   Otherwise the next model in the chain is tried.
2. Phone (`validAI()` in `src/agents.js`):
   - `hi` and `en` at most 400 characters each (800 when replying to the learner's own question, which gets a
     step-by-step answer of 3–5 short lines);
   - Jaanch may not call a wrong answer right (an English reply with "correct/right" and no negation is rejected);
   - while the learner is still trying (verdict not correct, attempt < 2), the reply may not reveal the answer:
     no "= 7", no bare answer number that is not already in the question, no easier sum that adds up to it
     ("5 + 3"), and no "3 more than 5" wording;
   - the free-text score is forced to an integer from 0 to 3.
3. The phone waits at most 11 s; offline it does not call at all.

**Fallback.** Any failure (offline, timeout, every model fails, a check fails) shows the scripted line written for that
exact situation in D3, which was written and checked in advance. Each message is logged as `agent_message` with
`source: ai | scripted` and the model name, so the teacher's Data tab shows the share of AI lines.

### F1. Jaanch (Evaluator): put the verdict into words
- **Does:** after every answer, says in one sentence whether it is right, exactly as the checker decided, and names
  the misconception in child-friendly words.
- **Input:** the blackboard JSON above, conversation empty (Jaanch speaks first). Role prompt:
```text
You are JAANCH, the Evaluator. The code checker's verdict and misconception tag are FINAL. Tell the learner, in one sentence, whether the answer is right (exactly as the verdict says), and if wrong name the likely misconception in child-friendly words (M1 = treated subtracting a negative like subtracting a positive; M2 = used "two minuses make a plus" where it does not apply). Do not explain the m
```
- **Output:** `{"hi", "en", "stance"}`. Real reply on the live app for T1 with answer +7 (M2), 2026-11-18, model
  `openai/gpt-oss-120b`: *"तुम्हारा उत्तर गलत है, क्योंकि तुम दो माइनस को प्लस मान रहे हो जहाँ नहीं होना चाहिए।"*
  (*"Your answer is wrong because you treated two minuses as a plus where it doesn't apply."*)
- **Check / fallback:** the checks above; scripted line, e.g. T1-M2 *"उत्तर +7 नहीं है। लगता है "दो माइनस = प्लस" वाला
  नियम यहाँ लग गया।"*

### F2. Samjhao (Explainer): a nudge targeted at the misconception
- **Does:** reads Jaanch's message and the tag, then gives one nudge for this item: the udhaar model for M1,
  number-line direction for M2.
- **Input:** the same JSON plus `conversation: [Jaanch's message]`. Role prompt:
```text
You are SAMJHAO, the Explainer. Jaanch diagnosed the misconception tag on the blackboard:
M1 = "subtracting always makes it smaller" → use the udhaar model (removing a debt raises your account).
M2 = "two minuses make a plus everywhere" → use number-line direction (adding a negative moves left).
"other"/"sign"/"diff" → point at the direction to move. Give a targeted nudge for THIS item, not a lecture.
```
- **Output:** `{"hi", "en", "stance"}`; `stance: "disagree"` labels the bubble "🤝 Disagrees with Jaanch".
- **Check / fallback:** the checks above (the no-answer-reveal rule matters most here); scripted line, e.g. T1-M2
  *"यहाँ ऋणात्मक संख्या जोड़ी जा रही है, घटाई नहीं जा रही। ₹4 उधार में ₹3 और उधार जुड़ा…"*

### F3. Sawaal (Challenger): one question or counterexample
- **Does:** after a correct answer (and on T6-M2), asks one "why?" or gives one counterexample, using the blackboard
  history ("in question 1…").
- **Input:** the same JSON plus the conversation so far. Role prompt:
```text
You are SAWAAL, the Challenger. Ask ONE short "why?" question, or give ONE counterexample or extension that tests whether the learner's reasoning generalises (e.g. does the rule still hold when a negative is ADDED?). If the blackboard history shows an earlier misconception, refer to that question number. Do not answer your own question. If Jaanch accepted a memorised rule, you may challenge Jaanch
```
- **Output / check / fallback:** as F2; scripted line, e.g. T1 correct *"एक सवाल: यहाँ भी दो माइनस थे, फिर भी उत्तर
  प्लस क्यों नहीं बना?"*

### F4. Learner asks a question ("Explain it to me" / "Or challenge me instead")
- **Does:** the learner types a question; it goes to Samjhao (main button) or Sawaal (small option) together with
  the conversation so far, as `learner_question` (max 200 characters).
- **Check:** the same checks, so the answer to the current question is still not revealed.
- **Fallback:** Samjhao → the item's first hint; Sawaal → *"अच्छा सवाल! पहले खुद सोचो: दाईं ओर जाना है या बाईं ओर?"*
  (*"Good question! First think: right or left?"*).

### F5. The disagreement (S4, T5 option B)
- **Does:** Jaanch (AI) judges the learner's shortcut reason "two minuses make a plus" and accepts it for this
  question. Its reply is passed to Sawaal with this extra instruction:
```text
Jaanch accepted the learner's memorised shortcut. As Sawaal you DISAGREE: explain in one sentence why a memorised rule is risky and name the counterexample −2 + (−5). Set stance to "disagree".
```
  The coordinator then shows one "Two views: you decide" card with three choices: test Sawaal's example
  (−2 + (−5) on the number line, checked by code), keep my reason, or ask my teacher.
- **Check / fallback:** the checks above; scripted Jaanch and Sawaal lines from D3 Part C. Sawaal's line about
  an earlier question ("in question N this rule went wrong") is scripted and comes from the blackboard.

### F6. Jaanch scores the learner's own explanation (T5, 0–3)
- **Does:** scores a free-text explanation of why 5 − (−3) = 8, in Hindi, Hinglish or English, and gives one
  encouraging next step. Role prompt:
```text
You are JAANCH, the Evaluator. Score the learner's free-text explanation of why 5 − (−3) = 8 on a 0–3 rubric:
+1 uses a model (number-line direction or udhaar/debt), +1 says subtracting a negative moves right or increases the value, +1 reaches 8 consistent with the reason.
The learner may write in Hindi, Hinglish (Roman Hindi) or English. Give ONE encouraging sentence naming what to add next.
Return ONLY JSON: {"score": <0-3 integer>, "hi": "<Hindi>", "en": "<English>"}
```
- **Output:** `{"score", "hi", "en"}`; shown as "… (score 2/3)" with the note "Your teacher will review this and may
  change it."
- **Check:** the score is clamped to an integer 0–3; text checks as above.
- **Fallback:** `rubricFallback()`, a keyword rubric (model word +1, direction/increase word +1, "8" +1) with a fixed
  tip per score.
- **Human check (C5):** every free-text score goes to the teacher's review queue, where the teacher approves the AI's
  feedback or overrides it with their own message, which the learner sees on S5.

### Known limitations
- The checks catch wrong verdicts and answer leaks, not every weak explanation; the scripted reference line in the
  prompt and teacher review are the mitigation.
- The teacher's review card for a disagreement stores the scripted Jaanch and Sawaal lines, not the exact AI text the
  learner saw.
- The conversation resets on each submit; memory across questions comes only from the blackboard.

# Ganit Chaupal: Design Rationale

The content (persona, outcomes, tasks, feedback) is in [REPORT.md](REPORT.md) sections D1–D3. This file holds the
design decisions and the build blueprint.

## Design principles

1. **DP1:** We will check every numeric answer with code and use the AI agents only to explain, question and phrase
   feedback, because Kavita has no one at home to cross-check a wrong AI explanation, and unverified AI output is an
   AIED anti-pattern.
2. **DP2:** We will show agent disagreement as one labelled "दो राय: तुम तय करो" card with three choices, instead of
   separate conflicting messages, because loose contradictions add extraneous load (CLT), while resolving the conflict
   herself drives conceptual change and keeps her in charge (autonomy, Self-Determination Theory).
3. **DP3:** We will teach every rule through two concrete models, a number-line move and an udhaar story, because she
   memorised "minus-minus-plus" without meaning (M2). A familiar village context plus a picture gives two routes to
   encoding (situated learning, dual coding).
4. **DP4:** We will give Samjhao's hint ladder (nudge → worked step → answer) before revealing any answer, because she
   has no tutor and learns best with just-enough help at the point of being stuck (ZPD).
5. **DP5:** We will design for a shared, weakly connected phone:
   - Hindi and English, one-tap toggle on every screen, remembered per phone (English is the default view)
   - one task per screen, no sound needed
   - a session of about 20 minutes; Pause shows a resume card (and pauses automatically when the phone is taken
     back), "Done for today" saves and exits
   - tasks and scripted feedback pre-loaded; events saved on the phone and synced later
   - AI with an 11-second limit and a fallback to scripted text

   We will do this because of L1's constraints (the phone gets taken back, evening data is weak) and because we saw
   Gemini return 503 errors and take about 10 seconds per call during the build.
6. **DP6:** We will send unresolved disagreements and every AI judgement of a free-text explanation to a teacher queue,
   where the teacher approves or overrides them before the next session, because the AI is least reliable on open
   answers and the teacher is the trusted authority (C5, human-in-the-loop).

## Theory → feature map

| Theory | Prediction for Kavita | Feature | Code location |
|---|---|---|---|
| Conceptual change / cognitive conflict | Two clashing rules need resolving with evidence | "दो राय" card + test item | `src/screens/TwoViews.jsx` |
| ZPD / scaffolding | Stuck with no tutor | Samjhao hint ladder; targeted re-explanation per misconception | `ROLES.samjhao` in `api/agent.js`; `task.hints` in `src/content.js` |
| Cognitive Load Theory | 30-minute window, small screen | 4 concept cards, one task per screen, at most 2 agent bubbles per turn | `src/screens/Learn.jsx`, `Practice.jsx` |
| Situated learning + dual coding | Rules without meaning | Number line + udhaar stories | `src/components/NumberLine.jsx`, `src/content.js` |
| Affective filter | Goes quiet when publicly wrong | Private, encouraging feedback; no scores shown to others | feedback text in `content.js` |
| Human-in-the-loop AIED (C5) | AI may misjudge free text | Teacher approve/override queue | `src/screens/Teacher.jsx`, `reviews` table |

## Multi-agent architecture (P3)

## Screens (D4): identity token `ID 23B2107 · S#` in the header of every screen

| ID | Screen | Learner or teacher input → system output | Next |
|---|---|---|---|

## Data
- **Storage:** localStorage first, then batch sync to Supabase. Tables: `events` (clickstream), `learners`, and a new
  `reviews` table for the teacher queue.
- **Events:** session_start, item_presented, answer_submitted (correct, misconception), hint_requested,
  agent_message (agent, source ai|scripted), disagreement_shown, disagreement_choice, teacher_review, session_end.

## Limitations
- The persona's details are assumed, not taken from field data.
- There is only one activity, and it covers addition and subtraction only (multiplication sign rules are left out).
- The Supabase read policy is open for the demo.

(4) Every AI line is validated;\nany failure shows the scripted line from D3. Agents exchange information through five channels: the conversation\n(each reply goes to the next agent), the shared blackboard, a stance field (\\emph{agree}/\\emph{disagree}, shown on the\nbubble), a debate flag (Jaanch's verdict handed to Sawaal to challenge), and the teacher queue.\n\n\\textbf{Model call.} One endpoint, \\texttt{/api/agent}. P3 – Multi-agent collaborative learning environment
AI agents · Collaborative learning · Scaffolding
Design an application where at least three AI agents perform distinct educational roles for your card's topic (for example, one explains, one challenges the learner's reasoning, one evaluates evidence and gives feedback). The agents must exchange information with each other to support the learner's progress.
Design challenge: How will the system prevent conflicting agent advice from confusing learners while keeping learner agency? Show one moment where two agents disagree and how the learner experiences it.


T1 Topic Integers: Integers: operations with negative numbers (Class 7)

L1 Learner context Class 6–8 student in a rural government school, regional-language medium, uses a parent's Android phone for about 30 minutes in the evening


C5
Teacher-in-the-loop
A teacher view that shows learner progress and lets the teacher approve or override AI feedback



5. Required deliverables
You submit a working hosted app plus a report with  Every part must be specific to your card. Placeholder text such as “AI generates a question” earns no marks: show the actual content and the actual feedback.

5. Required deliverables

D1
Educational problem
The problem for your topic and learner, in 3–5 sentences. Three measurable learning outcomes using action verbs (explain, predict, compare…). The context of use: where, when, on what device

----- [2026-11-18 13:53:46] ASSISTANT -----
Your exam app already tries several Gemini key/model pairs in order before giving up (`api/agent.js:7`), so the quickest fix is to put a second provider at the end of that list. These free options need no credit card:

| Provider | Setup | Why use it | Catch |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Groq** (best pick) | console.groq.com → sign in with Google → API Keys → Create | Very fast (often under 1 s), runs Llama 3.3 70B and others, and uses the OpenAI request format | Per-minute and per-day request limits, but they're generous enough for a demo |
| **Cerebras** | cloud.cerebras.ai → sign in → API key | Also very fast, also OpenAI format, large daily token allowance | Fewer models to choose from |
| **OpenRouter** | openrouter.ai → sign in → Keys | One key reaches many models. Use the ones whose names end in `:free` (e.g. `meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free`) | Low daily cap on free models (about 50 requests/day without credit). Free models can be slow or busy |
| **GitHub Models** | github.com/marketplace/models → use a GitHub token (PAT) | You already have a GitHub account. Includes GPT-4o-mini-class models | Strict daily limits |
| **Mistral** | console.mistral.ai → free "Experiment" plan | Decent quality | Needs phone verification |

Free-tier limits change often. These are from memory, so check the numbers on each console page.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Groq, Cerebras, OpenRouter and GitHub Models all accept the **OpenAI chat-completions format** (`POST /v1/chat/completions` with a `messages` array). One small `callOpenAICompat(baseURL, model, key)` function covers all four; only the base URL and model name change.
- Gemini's API uses a different format (`contents`/`parts`), so you'd need that one extra function next to `callGemini`. The rest of your fallback loop stays the same.
- For a live demo, Groq's speed matters more than its free quota. Your working Gemini model takes about 10 s per reply; Groq would usually make the 3-agent disagreement screen feel instant.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**To set up Groq:**
1. Get a key at console.groq.com.
2. Run `! vercel env add GROQ_API_KEY production` and paste the key when asked. Also add it to `.env.local`.
3. Say "go" and I'll add a Groq entry (`llama-3.3-70b-versatile`) to the fallback list, test it locally with curl, and redeploy. That's about 3 minutes.

Should Groq be the **first** choice (fast) or only a **fallback** (Gemini stays first)? For the demo I'd put Groq first.
